source: Han, Lan, Kilicoglu (2026) When Evidence Conflicts: Uncertainty and Order Effects in Retrieval-Augmented Biomedical QA
finding: Same two contradictory documents, order reversed, give different answers. The correct-first order beats the incorrect-first order in all six models.
numbers: HealthContradict, 6 open-weight LLMs, 920 paired predictions per model. Reversing order flips the answer for 11.4% to 25.2% of items (mean 18.6%). Mean accuracy gap correct-first vs incorrect-first 11.1 points; per model 2.1 (Qwen3.5-9B, p=0.0785, not significant) to 19.3 (Phi-4). Five of six significant (McNemar p<1e-7 for the five listed). Mean logit margin shift -1.40.
quote: reversing the two documents changes the predicted answer for 11.4%-25.2% of examples
limits: Small open-weight models only (about 4B-9B); one biomedical yes/no benchmark; two-document conflicts.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 8: LLM conflict judgments are order sensitive, with the same size (10-25%) as human glut order effects. In S6, show conflicting items in both orders and compare, or randomise order.

source: Han, Lan, Kilicoglu (2026) When Evidence Conflicts (accuracy and selective prediction results)
finding: Incorrect evidence hurts most, mixed evidence is in between. Raw confidence is a poor abstention signal under conflict, but a conflict-aware score (confidence drop against the correct-only condition) works better.
numbers: Mean accuracy: no context to correct-only 0.824 to 0.916; incorrect-only 0.425 (AUROC 0.477). Mean ECE 0.057 (correct-only) vs 0.456 (incorrect-only). Raw-confidence selective-accuracy gain in incorrect-only: -1.2, -0.9, -2.1 points at 75/50/25% coverage. Conflict-aware score: +7.2, +20.4, +33.4 points (incorrect-only); +3.6, +10.4, +14.4 (incorrect-correct-correct order).
limits: The conflict score needs a trained predictor and a clean reference condition; trained on the same benchmark's train split; yes/no biomedical items only.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 9: a conflict signal can drive abstention better than raw confidence, but it was a learned score, not a bilateral (for, against) pair. Supports using conflict as a trigger for verification at S6.

source: Gokul, Tenneti, Nakkiran (2025) Contradiction Detection in RAG Systems: LLMs as Context Validators
finding: Conflict type matters a lot. Contradictions between two documents are easiest to detect; contradictions inside one document are hardest. All models have high precision and low recall.
numbers: Claude-3 Sonnet, Claude-3 Haiku, Llama3.3-70B, Llama3.1-8B, basic vs CoT prompts. Self-contradiction detection accuracy 0.006 to 0.456 across models. Pair contradiction: Llama-70B basic 0.893, Sonnet CoT 0.831. Sonnet+CoT overall: accuracy 0.710, precision 0.951, recall 0.566; Sonnet basic: 0.539, 0.901, 0.296. Llama-70B basic 0.679 vs CoT 0.497. Haiku basic recall 0.036.
limits: Synthetic contradictions (LLM generated, quality control left for future work); 2024-era models; CoT effect sign flips by model family (+31% Sonnet, +46% Haiku, -26% Llama-70B).
agent_relevance: Closes gap 3 in part: ranking of conflict types by difficulty is self-contradiction (own trace or one document) worst, pair across sources easiest. S6 needs a dedicated self-consistency pass over its own trace because that is where detection is weakest.

source: Gokul, Tenneti, Nakkiran (2025) Contradiction Detection in RAG Systems (position and type-detection results)
finding: Distance between conflicting documents and prompt style change detection. CoT stabilises position effects. Naming the conflict type is not helped by CoT.
numbers: Claude-3 Sonnet basic: 18.8 points better accuracy when conflicting documents are far apart than near; with CoT the gap is 0.7 points. Type detection: CoT lowers performance by 8% (Claude) to 25% (Llama-70B).
limits: Same synthetic data and models as d03. Differences between prompt conditions come from single runs without reported confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 8 for the document case: position sensitivity exists but a reasoning step reduces it for one model. Randomise placement of conflicting items in S6 tests.

source: Cheng Jiayang et al. (2024) ECon: On the Detection and Resolution of Evidence Conflicts
finding: LLMs, NLI and factual-consistency models have high precision but weaker recall in detecting answer conflicts. Recall depends on prompt wording, precision does not.
numbers: Answer-conflict sensitivity to prompt wording (mean over wordings, short setting): Mixtral 8x7B precision 98.89, recall 23.35 (SD 3.46); Llama-3 8B 95.29 / 58.99; Llama-3 70B 98.07 / 69.74; Claude 3 Haiku 95.83 / 55.70; Claude 3 Sonnet 97.45 / 70.24. Long setting: Mixtral recall 24.07, Llama-3 70B 74.76, Sonnet 71.51.
limits: Conflicts are generated and validated pairs (NQ, CWQ based); only two-evidence pairs; models are 2024 era.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 3 reading: detection recall is the weak side everywhere, so S6 should not rely on one unprompted check. A forced conflict question raises recall.

source: Cheng Jiayang et al. (2024) ECon (input-order sensitivity, appendix Table 16)
finding: For strong LLMs, swapping the order of two evidence items changes conflict-detection F1 by only a few points. Mixtral moves more.
numbers: First dataset column, original vs reverse order F1: Mixtral 49.7 vs 46.9; Llama-3 70B 81.6 vs 80.6; Claude 3 Sonnet 82.4 vs 82.0; GPT-4 74.2 vs 75.6; Llama-3 8B 76.2 vs 74.4. The paper says most detectors are order sensitive and reports the average of both orders.
limits: The table is garbled in text extraction, so I read only the first dataset block; later columns not checked. Binary detection only, not resolution.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 8 with a counterpoint to d01: detection is only mildly order sensitive (0.4-2.8 F1 points) while resolution (which side wins) is strongly order sensitive (d01 11-25% flips). The order risk is in adjudication, not in noticing.

source: Cheng Jiayang et al. (2024) ECon (how LLMs resolve conflicts, Section 4)
finding: When shown conflicting evidence, LLMs often pick one side with no reason. Stronger conflict intensity makes models more likely to refrain; weak conflicts are merged.
numbers: Manually labelled resolution types: resolve by chance 24% (Sonnet) and 38% (Haiku). Without a prior belief, Sonnet: refrain 36.1%, content reliability 11.1%, internal knowledge 4.2%, chance 20.8%, integration 29.2%. Haiku with belief: chance 45.7%.
quote: LLMs often favor one piece of conflicting evidence without justification
limits: Small manual annotation (factoid conflicts); only Claude 3 Sonnet and Haiku annotated; the categories are subjective.
agent_relevance: Baseline data for gap 1: unprompted models mostly neither halt nor keep both; 24-38% choose silently at random. A kept (for, against) record plus an explicit adjudication line removes the silent choice.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) Exploring Knowledge Conflicts for Faithful LLM Reasoning: ConflictQA
finding: With text vs knowledge-graph evidence in conflict, LLMs lean on the compact triples and often use only one source. Reordering the evidence does not give a consistent fix.
numbers: 12 LLMs. Evidence-order gap (F1) in the non-complementary TripleConf setting: Qwen3-8B +19.74, Open-Mistral-7B +9.79, GPT-4o +4.14, GPT-5.1 -4.82, DeepSeek-V3.2 -7.71, Llama-3.1-8B -4.72. Reasoning LLMs show smaller order gaps than general LLMs.
quote: changing the evidence order does not consistently enable faithful reasoning across all LLMs
limits: Results elsewhere are averaged over two orders; one run per cell; conflicts are built by corrupting one source.
agent_relevance: Extends gap 8 and gap 3 to cross-source conflicts: the sign of the order effect depends on the model, so the scaffold cannot assume one fixed order is safe.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) ConflictQA, XoT two-stage explanation-based thinking
finding: XoT first lists every candidate answer with an explanation tied to its source, then decides in a second step. This is a kept-both-sides record followed by adjudication, and it beat direct and conflict-aware prompts.
numbers: Complementary setting with misleading KG: GPT-4o relative gain about 20% in F1 and in exact match over the conflict-aware QA prompt. Open-Mistral-7B F1 almost 3x (183% relative F1 gain, 100% EM gain in complementary). Qwen3-8B +111% relative F1 non-complementary. Gains under TextConf are model dependent, and reasoning models gain less.
limits: Compared with direct, CoT and a conflict-aware prompt, not with repair-by-retraction or halting, and not at equal tokens (XoT adds a second call). One benchmark built by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest existing test for gap 1: keep both candidates with sourced explanations then adjudicate beats no-record prompting. It does not settle keep vs retract vs halt and does not control tokens, so gap 1 stays open.

source: Dhanda (2026) DeltaLogic: minimal premise edits reveal belief-revision failures (reopened for edit types)
finding: Models do well on fixed premises but fail to revise after support is removed or a defeating fact arrives. Adding a supporting premise is easy.
numbers: Log-likelihood label scoring (True/False/Uncertain), no CoT. 30-episode Qwen subset: Qwen3-1.7B initial 0.667, revised 0.467, inertia 0.600; Qwen3-0.6B revised 0.400 only through abstention 1.000. 20-episode subset: Qwen3-4B 0.650 / 0.450 / inertia 0.600; Phi-4-mini 0.950 / 0.850 / inertia 0.200, with over-flip and abstention nonzero. Qwen3-1.7B: perfect on support-insertion, fails completely on support-removal and defeating-fact edits. Qwen3-4B 0.000 on ProofWriter support-removal vs Phi-4-mini 0.667.
limits: Tiny N (20 and 30 episodes), four small models, workshop paper, no dependency-tracking or retraction method tested, so it does not compare adaptive-logic retraction with full re-solve.
agent_relevance: Partly informs gap 6: failure is concentrated on edits that remove support or defeat a belief, which is where dependency tracking would act. No paper tested retraction vs re-solve, so gap 6 stays open.

source: Allen et al. (2025) Sound and Complete Neurosymbolic Reasoning with LLM-Grounded Interpretations (reopened, Table 1 and discussion)
finding: The bilateral F1 gain is measured against a unilateral judge forced to answer on every item. The two are not matched on coverage, and the authors frame the trade as selective classification.
numbers: Unilateral coverage 1.000 on all four cells. Bilateral coverage 0.589 (GPQA flagship), 0.504 (GPQA distilled), 0.584 (SimpleQA flagship), 0.499 (SimpleQA distilled). F1 0.699 vs 0.633, 0.608 vs 0.559, 0.736 vs 0.657, 0.624 vs 0.570. Bootstrap SEs about 0.007-0.011 (1000 subsamples, N=100).
quote: This trade-off is not a limitation but a feature
limits: No unilateral baseline with an abstention threshold at 0.5-0.6 coverage and no self-consistency baseline in the paper. Verified by reading the table and discussion text.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open and is sharper: the missing control is a unilateral judge that abstains on its least confident 40-50% of items. Until then treat the 0.06 F1 gain as possibly a selective-classification effect.

source: Allen et al. (2025) (glut shares by model family and topic, bilateral truth value distributions)
finding: Glut rates are model-specific and topic-specific signatures, not one calibration constant. The authors argue gluts reflect real inconsistency in the LLM's knowledge and gaps reflect failed verbalization.
numbers: Zero-shot SimpleQA, ten topics. GPT family glut 59.0%, gap under 0.1%. Claude family glut 19.6%, gap 30.4%. Llama glut 52.9%, verified-only (t,f) 29.8%. Topics: Video games 63.6% glut, Sports 47.3%, History 35.7% (lowest, cross-model SD 15.0).
limits: The claim that gluts are genuine inconsistency is argued, not tested: no ablation of prompt wording or temperature on glut rate, and no check of whether gluts predict wrong answers. 2024-era models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly answered: glut share varies 19.6% to 59.0% by family, so a fixed glut threshold cannot be a universal trigger. Calibrate per model and topic, then use glut as a trigger for tool verification (untested).

source: Li, Li, Chang, Wu (2025) PCBench (reopened for token cost of instructed vs unprompted critique)
finding: Reasoning models that do not report a flawed premise unprompted spend many more tokens than when told to check premises. An explicit instruction raises reporting and lowers cost.
numbers: Easy set, output tokens original / unprompted-flawed / instructed-flawed. DeepSeek-R1: 956 / 2590 / 1014 (PPCCR 2.71, APCCR 1.06); critique rate 19.6% to 67.7%. o3-mini: 328 / 1279 / 1023 (PPCCR 3.90, APCCR 3.11); 14.4% to 73.2%. Claude-3.7-sonnet: 414 / 669 / 494; 36.2% to 69.8%. Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking 38.2% to 77.9%. o4-mini 4.0% to 74.2%.
limits: The instruction told the model to check premises; it is not the same as a one-line conflict register inside a normal solve. Easy subset only for token numbers; I matched the token columns to rows by arithmetic with the cost ratios because the table text is interleaved.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 4 largely: a forced check is cheaper, not dearer, in tokens for reasoning models (R1 about 2.6x fewer tokens) and raises reporting 3.5x to 18x. Adopt a mandatory conflict line at S6 entry; it still needs a test on our own task mix.

source: Jeripity Venkata (2026) Do Models Know Why They Changed Their Mind? CoT under knowledge conflict
finding: When a model flips between following a conflicting document and its own memory, the stated reasoning is almost the same either way. Only the self-rated confidence carries a weak signal.
numbers: 200 PopQA items, 8 models, 4 prompt conditions. Flip pairs keep 96% of same-answer reasoning similarity (cosine 0.784 vs 0.817, d=0.34; ROUGE-L d=0.45). Confidence tracks whether the model knew the fact r=0.134 (about 2% of variance). Only GPT-4o has reliable reasoning-decision coupling (beta -0.132, 95% CI -0.188 to -0.077). Native thinking tokens show more decision sensitivity than user-facing CoT (Wilcoxon p=0.033).
limits: Single independent author, preprint; parametric-vs-document conflict, not conflict between sources; similarity metrics are embedding based; some rates flagged by the author as upper bounds.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 4: a conflict can be resolved silently, and the written argument is a poor audit channel. Require a separate structured conflict line and a confidence value, not a prose rationale.

source: Yuksel et al. (2026) thinking-token vs stated-output acknowledgment of injected signals (as cited in Jeripity Venkata 2026)
finding: Across twelve reasoning models, thinking tokens acknowledge influential injected signals far more often than the final stated output does.
numbers: 87.5% in thinking tokens vs 28.6% in stated outputs (twelve reasoning models), second-hand.
limits: Second-hand via a citing paper; the primary paper was not opened. Do not cite the numbers as verified.
agent_relevance: Consistent with PCBench and Fan et al. for gap 4: noticing happens in the trace but is dropped from the answer. A forced report line moves it to the output.

source: Synthesis for gap 3: conflict type vs detection rate (d03, d05, PCBench c09/c10, WikiContradict a19, DRAGged c12)
finding: Across sources I opened: explicit between-source contradictions are detected well when asked and badly when not asked; implicit and self-contradictions are hardest.
numbers: Explicit vs implicit (WikiContradict, Llama-3-70b with cue) 60.0% vs 17.6%; self-contradiction accuracy 0.006-0.456 (d03); unprompted critique 4.0-40.5% (PCBench). Detection prompts: precision above 0.9 and recall as low as 0.036 (d03).
limits: This line is a synthesis of lines opened earlier (d03, d05, c09, c12, a19); no new source was opened for it, so opened is false.
agent_relevance: Priority for S6: (1) own-trace self-contradiction, (2) implicit conflicts that need deduction, (3) explicit between-source conflicts. Put the forced check first on the first two.

source: Su et al. (2024) ConflictBank: knowledge conflicts benchmark (search snippet only)
finding: Evidence order was randomised to avoid sequence effects; larger LLaMA2 models were more affected by where the conflicting content sat.
limits: Seen in a search snippet only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Another hint for gap 8 that order sensitivity appears in conflict tasks; cite d01, d04, d06, d08 instead.

source: Search log for gap 7: 2020-2026 LLM papers on LP, FDE, LFI, Belnap scaffolds (negative result with caveats)
finding: The re-run found no new paper that uses LP, FDE, LFI or Belnap four-valued logic as an LLM scaffold beyond Allen et al. The only other near hit was a non-LLM paper on abductive reasoning in a paraconsistent framework (arXiv 2408.07287, snippet only).
numbers: arXiv export, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs all returned HTTP 429 on this pass. Web search: 4 queries ran with results, the rest were refused (shared budget used up). Allen et al. (2507.09751, several versions and the journal copy) was the only direct hit.
limits: Search coverage is thin because of rate limits; absence is weak evidence. A rerun after quotas reset is needed before calling K25 established.
agent_relevance: Treat the novelty claim (no direct test of paraconsistent scaffolds for LLM agents) as probable but not proven.

finding: No source found that tests a da Costa style verified flag that limits classical inference to marked facts, or that compares dependency-based retraction with full re-solve, or that tests a paraconsistent checker on defeasible rulebreaker items.
numbers: 0 hits in the usable web searches on these topics. Closest items: DeltaLogic (d10, no retraction method), Allen et al. (d11, gluts detected but no restricted-inference ablation), Rulebreakers (earlier lines c06-c08, logic checkers hurt).
limits: Negative result under tool limits (APIs at 429, web search budget gone). Not a proof of absence.
agent_relevance: These three remain open design questions; treat them as internal agent experiments, not as settled by the literature.
